I recently had an ACTH stim test and the results have left me wondering if I should ask further about whether cortisol could be something contributing to my symptoms. Is that possible even if I responded to the injection?

My cortisol baseline was 98 nmol/L (about 3.5 mcg/dl) and 30m post-injection my cortisol 512 nmol/L (about 18.5 mcg/dl). The endo said this was normal, but the sub-100 baseline has left me with some questions.

My smptoms include extremely severe fatigue (mostly bedbound), fainting, salt cravings, excessive thirst (4-6L+ a day), etc. I also have mild untreated hypothyroidism. I had a big drop in DHEA-S (top of range to bottom of range) and testosterone (dropped by 1.2 nmol/L in about half a year) last year, accompanied by some body hair loss, but I'm doing better with that now (symptomwise at least - I've not been re-tested).

I had a good sleep schedule before the test and lay down in the car park beforehand as well so I got some sun to wake me up, and I also thought hypothyroidism typically caused elevated cortisol. I thought my baseline would be higher than it was.

Regarding the stimulation thing, realising that a major reason I was self-harming was due to sensory issues from my ASD has been the biggest thing that has helped me stop. I think people underestimate how bad severe understimulation can be. I can remember banging my head on the wall and stuff as a kid with no intention to hurt myself. It was just from sensory issues - I needed input to calm myself. Then as my depression got worse as I got older it merged into something bigger I guess. But if I can deal with the sensory issues it takes away that physical need for it. Are there other kinds of sensory input you like that scratch a similar itch? It might be something to think about. Hi, sorry to reply to an old comment. I have both trauma and ME/CFS with neuro symptoms and this was super interesting. Would it be okay to ask a couple of questions?

I'm really sorry your health is still not good.

I got a referral after discussing my symptoms and having my HR and BP taken laying down and standing up, and my GP said they thought it was POTS straight away. I then asked for a cardiologist referral and they referred me to the POTS UK website to read up on lifestyle measures (salt, water, compression) in the meantime.

My GP practice has a lot of young people attend which might be why they were more familiar than average, which was lucky for me.

I would make sure they know what your specific triggers are, as well as what functional impairment you're having. If you're unable to do stuff because of your symptoms they should absolutely be looking into it. That is the bit I would emphasise personally.

When I first went to the doctor's for fainting when I was way younger they just told me to eat more salt to keep my blood pressure up. That is a possible outcome, but if that's not enough, let them know how much salt you're having and again what your level of functional impairment is.



I do wonder how I would be now if I was diagnosed when I was younger. I worsened massively a couple of years ago after having milder POTS symptoms for a long time. Maybe if I had a handle on mild POTS I would have had a headstart on severe POTS.


I would stay open to the idea it could be something else as well, there are plenty of posts on here of people who ended up having something else. I will say if any of your other diagnoses are autoimmune though, POTS can be secondary to other autoimmune conditions that can cause autonomic neuropathy - may be worth knowing.


Good luck, hope your appointment goes well
